title: Energy by the numbers: how much there is, and how fast it comes

summary.text: One chapati holds about as much energy as seven phone batteries, yet eating one does not charge you up in a minute. Your body lets the energy out slowly, at about the pace of a bright bulb. Your child measures their own energy on a staircase, counts the blinks of the home electricity meter, and learns two ideas that are easy to mix up. Joules say how much energy there is. Watts say how fast it moves. They find out why a small fan left on all night can use more energy than a big kettle, and how the energy in sunlight, in food and in electricity can all be counted in the same unit.
summary.art: A steel plate with one chapati on it beside a phone on charge, with a thin line of golden numbers joining them, and a ceiling fan turning above.

intro.hook: Switch on a ceiling fan and a kettle. The kettle is much more powerful, yet the fan can cost you more in a night. How can a gentle fan use more than a fierce kettle?
intro.text: To answer that, you need to ask two different questions. How much energy is there? And how fast does it move? In this unit you climb a staircase against a stopwatch, and you turn your own climb into numbers. You watch the little light on the electricity meter blink as appliances switch on. Then you find out how a chapati, a battery and a sunny window can all be counted in one unit.
intro.art: A child at the bottom of a staircase holding a phone stopwatch, while a parent waits at the top, and a ceiling fan and an electric kettle are drawn small in the corner.

outcomes: I can name the forms of energy (movement, heat, light, sound, electrical and stored) and say which one I am seeing in a thing at home.
I can explain that joules count how much energy there is and watts count how fast it moves, and give an example of each.
I can measure my own energy and power on a staircase, and work out joules and watts from my measurements.
I can read a rating plate and an electricity meter, and work out how much energy an appliance uses in a given time.
I can explain why a small-watt appliance left on for hours can use more energy than a big-watt appliance used for minutes.
I can explain that energy is never used up, but spreads out, and name the useful and the spread-out energy in a bulb or a fan.
I can tell how James Joule showed that movement can turn into heat, so both can be counted in the same unit.

terms.meaning: What is needed to make anything happen: to move, heat up, light up or make a sound.
terms.example: A fan needs energy from the wall socket to turn.
terms.art: A ceiling fan turning with a plug and wire leading to a wall socket.

terms.meaning: A name for what the energy is doing right now, such as movement, heat, light, sound, electrical or stored.
terms.example: In a lit torch, the cell holds stored energy, the wires carry electrical energy, and the bulb gives out light and a little heat.
terms.art: A torch with four small labels pointing to the cell, the wire, the bulb's light and the warm bulb.

terms.meaning: The unit for counting how much energy there is. The short sign is J.
terms.example: Lifting a 100 gram apple up by 1 metre takes about 1 joule.
terms.art: A child lifting an apple one metre up beside a ruler, with the number 1 J written near it.

terms.meaning: 1,000 joules. The short sign is kJ. Some food labels print it next to kilocalories.
terms.example: A small biscuit packet label may say 400 kilojoules.
terms.art: The back of a biscuit packet with a table of numbers and the word kilojoule circled.

terms.meaning: An older unit for food energy. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. People often just say calorie.
terms.example: One chapati holds about 100 kilocalories, which is about 420 kilojoules.
terms.art: A chapati on a plate with two number tags, 100 kilocalories and 420 kilojoules.

terms.meaning: How fast energy moves from one place to another, or from one form to another.
terms.example: A kettle changes energy much faster than a fan, so the kettle has more power.
terms.art: A kettle and a fan side by side, with a thick arrow from the kettle and a thin arrow from the fan.

terms.meaning: The unit for power. One watt means one joule of energy moving every second. The short sign is W.
terms.example: A 9 watt bulb takes 9 joules from the wall every second.
terms.art: An LED bulb with a clock beside it and the words 9 joules every second.

terms.meaning: The energy a 1,000 watt appliance uses in one hour. An electricity bill calls it one unit. It is 3.6 million joules.
terms.example: A 1,000 watt iron left on for one hour uses one unit.
terms.art: A clothes iron with a clock showing one hour and a bill with the word unit circled.

terms.meaning: The box on the wall that counts how much electrical energy your home has used. Newer ones have a small light that blinks.
terms.example: The light on the meter blinks faster when you switch on a geyser.
terms.art: A white energy meter box on a wall with a small red light blinking.

terms.meaning: The label on an appliance that tells its power in watts. It is the most the appliance will use.
terms.example: A mixer grinder may say 500 W on its rating plate.
terms.art: The underside of a mixer grinder with a silver label showing a number and the letter W.

terms.meaning: The part of the energy that does the job you wanted.
terms.example: In a bulb, the light is the useful energy.
terms.art: A bulb with a bright wide arrow of light labelled useful.

terms.meaning: The part of the energy that ends up as warmth in the air and in things around, too thin to gather and use again. People often call it wasted energy.
terms.example: A bulb is warm to the touch. That warmth is spread-out energy.
terms.art: A bulb with thin faint arrows of warmth spreading into the air around it.

terms.meaning: Giving a lot of useful energy for the energy you put in.
terms.example: An LED bulb is more efficient than an old filament bulb, because more of its energy becomes light.
terms.art: Two bulbs side by side, an LED with a big light arrow and a filament bulb with a small light arrow and a big heat arrow.

terms.meaning: The rule that energy is never made or destroyed. It only moves or changes form. The total stays the same.
terms.example: When a ball is dropped, the stored energy it had from being held up high turns into movement, then into sound and warmth. The total stays the same.
terms.art: A ball falling in three pictures, with a bar of energy changing colour but staying the same length.

explanations.description: You never see energy by itself. You see what it is doing. Movement energy is in anything that is moving, such as a rolling marble. Heat energy is in the jiggling of the tiny particles in a warm thing. Light and sound carry energy across a room. Electrical energy flows through wires. Stored energy waits in food, in a stretched rubber band, and in a ball held up high. A form is a name for what the energy is doing right now. One thing can show several forms at once. A lit LED bulb takes in electrical energy and gives out light and a little heat.
examples: A rolling marble shows movement energy.
A hot tea shows heat energy.
A chapati holds stored energy, in the way its atoms are joined, until you eat it.
explanations.art: A torch with arrows from the cell (stored), the wire (electrical), the bulb (light) and the warm glass (heat).
explanations.definition: Energy is what is needed to make anything happen. Its forms are the different ways we notice it: movement, heat, light, sound, electrical and stored.

explanations.concept: The joule: one unit for every form
explanations.description: Movement, heat, light and sound feel like different things, but they can be counted with the same unit. That is what makes the idea of energy useful. You can say how many joules a falling stone has, how many joules a cup of hot tea gave to the air, and how many joules a chapati holds. Lifting a 100 gram apple by 1 metre takes about 1 joule. Lifting a 1 kilogram bottle by 1 metre takes about 10 joules, because the bottle is ten times heavier than the apple and needs ten times as much energy. A kilojoule is 1,000 joules. Food labels also use kilocalories. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules.
examples: Lifting a 1 litre bottle of water by 1 metre takes about 10 joules.
One kilojoule is the energy of lifting a 1 litre bottle of water by 1 metre, 100 times.
A chapati of 100 kilocalories is about 420 kilojoules.
explanations.art: A bottle being lifted one metre on a ruler, with 10 J written, and a chapati with 420 kJ written.
explanations.definition: The joule is the unit scientists use for counting energy in every form. One joule is about the energy needed to lift a 100 gram apple up by 1 metre.

explanations.concept: A ladder of amounts: how much is that?
explanations.description: Lifting an apple by a metre is about 1 joule. Lifting a bottle of water by a metre is about 10 joules. An ordinary AA cell, the small kind in a remote, holds roughly 10 kilojoules. A phone battery holds about 60 kilojoules. One banana or one chapati holds about 400 kilojoules, which is seven times the phone battery. A unit of electricity, the kind on your bill, is 3.6 million joules, and it equals the food energy of about nine chapatis. A litre of petrol holds about 32 million joules. Big numbers like these are why we use kilo for a thousand and mega for a million.
examples: A chapati holds about as much energy as 7 phone batteries.
One unit of electricity is about as much energy as 9 chapatis.
A litre of petrol holds about 75 times as much energy as one chapati.
explanations.art: A ladder standing against a wall with rungs labelled with an apple, a bottle, a cell, a phone, a chapati, an electricity unit and a petrol can.
explanations.definition: Everyday things hold very different amounts of energy, from one joule to millions of joules. If you line them up like the rungs of a ladder, each rung is about ten times the one below.

explanations.description: Joules and watts answer two different questions. Joules ask how much. Watts ask how fast. Think of water. A litre is an amount. A litre every minute is a rate. A tap that drips and a tap that gushes can fill the same bucket, but the gushing tap does it in less time. A 9 watt bulb takes 9 joules from the wall every second. A 1,500 watt kettle takes 1,500 joules every second, which is more than 160 times as fast. Two machines can do the same job and use the same joules, but the more powerful one finishes sooner.
examples: A ceiling fan of 60 watts takes 60 joules each second.
A mixer grinder of 500 watts takes 500 joules each second.
When you climb the stairs fast, you might make 100 to 200 watts for a few seconds.
explanations.art: A bucket filling under a drip and under a gushing tap, with the words amount and rate.
explanations.definition: Power is how fast energy moves or changes form. Its unit is the watt. One watt means 1 joule of energy every second.

explanations.description: A 60 watt fan running for 10 hours uses 60 times 10, which is 600 watt-hours. A 1,500 watt kettle running for 4 minutes runs for one fifteenth of an hour, so it uses 1,500 divided by 15, which is 100 watt-hours. So the gentle fan uses six times as much energy as the fierce kettle. Time matters as much as power. Electricity bills count in kilowatt-hours, called units. One kilowatt-hour is a 1,000 watt appliance running for one hour, or a 100 watt one running for ten hours. To find the units, multiply watts by hours and divide by 1,000.
examples: A 9 watt LED bulb on for 10 hours uses 90 watt-hours.
A 2,000 watt geyser on for 30 minutes uses 1,000 watt-hours, which is one unit.
A 60 watt fan on for 16 hours uses 960 watt-hours, a little less than one unit.
explanations.art: A fan with a long clock bar of ten hours beside a kettle with a very short clock bar of four minutes, and the two energy totals drawn as boxes.
explanations.definition: The energy an appliance uses is its power multiplied by the time it runs. A bigger power or a longer time both mean more energy.

explanations.concept: You are a machine of about 100 watts
explanations.description: A day of eating gives a grown-up around 1,800 to 2,200 kilocalories. That is roughly 8 million joules. Spread over a day of 86,400 seconds, it comes to about 90 to 100 joules every second. Most of it becomes warmth, which is why a room full of people feels warm. When you climb stairs, your muscles turn only about one quarter of the food energy they use into lifting you. The other three quarters become heat. So when you lift yourself at 100 watts, your body is using about 400 watts for those seconds. Your body uses its energy slowly and steadily, in tiny steps in every cell.
examples: A person sitting in a closed room warms it like an old 100 watt bulb.
Climbing stairs fast may use 400 watts of food energy for a few seconds.
A marathon runner keeps going for hours because they spend energy at a rate their body can keep up.
explanations.art: A child sitting on a stool with a faint orange glow around them like a bulb, and a thermal camera style picture beside it.
explanations.definition: A resting grown-up uses food energy at about 80 to 100 watts all day, and a child a little less. Hard work makes it more.

explanations.description: A filament bulb turns only a few out of every 100 joules into light. The rest is warmth, which is why the bulb is hot to touch. An LED bulb turns many more of its joules into light, so a 9 watt LED gives about as much light as an old 60 watt filament bulb. A fan motor turns most of its energy into moving air but also warms up a little. Every machine, and every body, has some spread-out energy. We say the energy is wasted when it did nothing we wanted. It is not gone. It is in the air, as warmth that is too thin to use again.
examples: An LED bulb is more efficient than a filament bulb.
A phone charger feels warm because some of its energy spreads out as heat.
A cooking pot on a gas flame wastes the heat that goes round its sides.
explanations.art: Two bulbs, a filament one with a thin yellow light arrow and a big red heat arrow, and an LED with a big yellow light arrow and a small red heat arrow.
explanations.definition: In every change, some energy does the job you wanted and the rest spreads out as warmth. The useful share is called the efficiency.

explanations.description: When a moving cycle stops, its movement energy has not disappeared. The brakes and the road are slightly warmer, and the air is a little warmer. Scientists have counted this again and again, and the total always matches. People say energy is used up when they mean it has spread out too thin to use again. A ball dropped on the floor bounces lower each time because a share of its energy goes into sound and warmth at each bounce, but if you could count all of it, the total would still be the same. This rule is called the conservation of energy.
examples: A rolling ball stops because friction turns its movement into warmth.
A phone battery that is flat has given its energy to light, sound and warmth.
Rubbing your palms makes them warm, and the warmth comes from the movement of your hands.
explanations.art: A ball bouncing three times, with a bar under each bounce showing the energy split into movement, sound and warmth, always the same total length.
explanations.definition: Energy is never made and never destroyed. It moves from one place to another and changes form, and the total stays the same.

explanations.concept: Almost all the energy we use comes from the Sun
explanations.description: A patch of sunny floor one metre by one metre receives about as much power as a 1,000 watt heater, though the sun feels gentler because the light is spread out and the heat spreads away. In one hour, the sunlight that reaches the Earth carries roughly as much energy as all the people on Earth use in a whole year. Food, wind, rain, firewood, coal and petrol all hold energy that came from sunlight, either lately or long ago. We count their energy in joules, so we can compare them with the Sun's light using the same unit.
examples: A solar panel of one square metre may give about 150 to 200 watts of electricity at noon.
Wind is moving air that the Sun warmed unevenly.
Coal and petrol hold energy that came from sunlight, through plants and sea creatures that lived millions of years ago.
explanations.art: The Sun with long rays reaching a flat roof with a square metre marked on it and the number 1,000 W.
explanations.definition: The Sun sends out about 380 trillion trillion watts. At noon on a clear day, about 1,000 watts of its light reaches each square metre of the ground.

explanations.description: The physicist Richard Feynman told a story about a child with 28 blocks. Each day the child's mother counts them and finds 28, even though some are hidden in a box, in a toy, or under the rug. She finds them by working out a sum. Feynman said energy is like that. It is a number that stays the same, and we find it by adding up all the forms. He wrote that we do not know what energy is. Some physicists say energy is only that number, a way of keeping the books. Others say it is real stuff, held in fields and in matter, and that Einstein's equation E = mc² shows mass is energy too. Scientists still argue about this.
examples: Counting energy always works, in toys, stars and cells.
Einstein's equation E = mc² says that mass is a store of energy, and that even a very small mass holds a huge amount of energy.
Nobody knows why the total of energy never changes, though one idea ties it to the laws of nature working the same on every day.
explanations.art: A child looking at 28 blocks, some in a box and some under a rug, with a notebook that says 28.

perspectives.explanation: Energy is a number we calculate. It stays the same in every change. We do not know what energy is, only how to count it.
Energy is a real property of matter and fields, like how fast something moves. Mass itself is a store of energy, as E = mc² says.

explanations.definition: Physicists can count energy exactly and it always adds up. Nobody has a final answer to what energy is underneath.

agreed.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. It moves and changes form, and the total stays the same.
agreed.evidence: Careful measurements, from Joule's paddle wheel in the 1840s to modern power stations, always find the same total.

agreed.text: Joules count how much energy there is. Watts count how fast it moves. One watt is one joule every second.
agreed.evidence: These are the agreed units of science worldwide, written into the International System of Units.

agreed.text: The energy an appliance uses equals its power times the time it runs.
agreed.evidence: Electricity meters work this way. They add up watts over time and show the result in units, or kilowatt-hours.

agreed.text: Most of the energy in food ends up as warmth in the body and in the air.
agreed.evidence: A resting person warms a closed room, and a crowded hall gets warmer, just as the same number of 100 watt bulbs would warm it.

agreed.text: A machine can change only part of its energy into the form you want. The rest spreads out as warmth.
agreed.evidence: Bulbs, fans, phone chargers and car engines all get warm when they work.

agreed.text: Nearly all the energy we use traces back to sunlight. The exceptions are nuclear power and some heat from deep in the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Food, wind, rain, coal, oil and gas can be followed back to the Sun. Nuclear power and geothermal heat can not.

challenging.for: A battery goes flat, a car runs out of petrol and you feel tired after a run.
challenging.against: The energy did not vanish. It moved into light, movement, sound and warmth around us. What runs out is energy in a form we can use.

challenging.claim: The more energy something holds, the more powerful it is.
challenging.who: Many students, because the two words sound alike.
challenging.for: A powerful engine usually holds a lot of fuel.
challenging.against: A chapati holds more energy than a phone battery, but a phone battery gives out its energy much faster. Energy is how much. Power is how fast.

challenging.claim: An appliance with more watts always costs more to run.
challenging.for: A geyser of 2,000 watts uses far more energy each minute than a fan of 60 watts.
challenging.against: Cost depends on watts times hours. A fan left on for 16 hours can use more than a geyser used for 20 minutes.

challenging.claim: Energy is a kind of stuff that flows from one thing to another.
challenging.who: Scientists before the 1840s thought heat was an invisible fluid called caloric.
challenging.for: Heat does seem to flow from a hot cup into cold hands, and the amount seems to stay the same as it moves.
challenging.against: Joule showed that heat can be made out of movement, so heat is not a fluid. Many physicists today say energy is a number we keep, not a substance. Others say it is a real property of matter and fields.

challenging.claim: The number on a food label is exactly the energy your body gets.
challenging.who: Most food labels and diet apps.
challenging.for: Labels are made by burning foods and adding up standard values for protein, fat and carbohydrate. These give good averages.
challenging.against: How much you actually get depends on how the food is cooked and chewed, and on the tiny living beings in your gut. Two people can get different amounts from the same chapati.

big_questions.q: A chapati holds the energy of seven phone batteries, but you cannot charge a phone by eating one. What does the body do that a charger cannot?
big_questions.hint: Think about the form the energy is in, and how fast it can be let out.

big_questions.q: If energy is never used up, why do we worry about running out of it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between energy that can still do a job and energy that has spread out as warmth.

big_questions.q: Is energy a thing, or a number we keep? Which would you say, and what would change your mind?
big_questions.hint: Think about Feynman's 28 blocks, and about what you could count in the Stair Power experiment.

big_questions.q: Your body lets out food energy at about 100 watts. Why is that good, and what would happen if it came out all at once?
big_questions.hint: Think about a chapati burned on a plate, compared with a chapati eaten over a day.

big_questions.q: Who decides how much electricity a family 'needs'? Does a family in a flat in Chennai need the same as a family in a village without a fridge?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the energy is used for, and about who has a choice.

big_questions.q: Women in many Indian homes spend hours cooking over a fire or a stove each day. Does the energy meter count their work?
big_questions.hint: Think about human energy as well as electricity, and what a meter can and cannot measure.

big_questions.q: The Sun sends the Earth in one hour as much energy as people use in a year. Why do we not simply use it all?
big_questions.hint: Think about catching it, storing it, and sharing it with plants and every other living being.

big_questions.q: A bee, a bat and you each sense a different part of the light and sound around you. Is the energy in the light the same for all three, or does each of you get a different energy?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is in the light itself, and what each body can catch.

story.title: The Night Mini Did the Sums
story.note: A made-up story. The people and the building are imagined. The numbers are real kinds of numbers: watt ratings like these are common on rating plates, and a battery really does hold a fixed number of watt-hours. A breathing machine, called an oxygen concentrator, often uses about 300 watts, but models differ.
text: The rain had been falling over Kochi for three days when the lights went out. It was ten o'clock at night. The whole street went dark at once, and the fans in every flat slowed and stopped.
Mini was ten. She stood at the window of the fourth-floor flat and watched the last light go from the road. 'Ammamma,' she said, 'the lift has stopped. And the pump.'
'The building has a big battery for nights like this,' said Ammamma. 'Go and see what Pillai Uncle is doing.'

In the small room by the stairs, Mr. Pillai, the secretary of the building, was bending over a grey box with a glowing number on it. A torch was clamped under his arm. Three neighbours stood behind him, all speaking at once.

'The battery has three thousand watt-hours,' said Mr. Pillai. 'That should last all night. I will switch on the lift, so nobody has to climb. And I will run the water pump for an hour, so the tanks are full by morning.'
Mini read the number on the box. 'Three thousand watt-hours,' she said. 'Uncle, what is a watt-hour?'
Mr. Pillai looked surprised. 'It is how much energy the battery holds.'

'My teacher says a watt is one joule every second,' said Mini. 'So a watt-hour must be the energy a thing uses when it takes one watt for one hour. If you run a thing that takes ten watts, the battery gives it ten watt-hours every hour. Is that right?'
'Yes,' said Mr. Pillai slowly. 'That is right.'
'Then we can work out how long it lasts. We divide.' She took a pencil from behind her ear. She always carried one. 'But first we must know what we need. Who needs the power tonight?'

A thin voice came from the stairs. It was Annamma Aunty from the third floor. She leaned on the rail, with her daughter holding her arm. 'My machine,' she said. 'The breathing machine. It needs power all night. The doctor says I must not be without it.'
Nobody spoke. Everyone knew Annamma Aunty slept with a small grey machine that hummed beside her bed.
'How many watts is it?' asked Mini.
Annamma Aunty's daughter ran up the stairs and came back with the label from the back of the machine. 'Three hundred watts,' she said.
Mini wrote on the back of an electricity bill. '300 watts for 8 hours. That is 300 times 8. That is 2,400 watt-hours.' She looked up. 'That is almost the whole battery.'
'Then switch off everything else,' said one of the neighbours.

'Not everything,' said Mini. 'The battery has 3,000. The machine takes 2,400. That leaves 600.' She wrote it down. 'The lights on the stairs are LEDs, eight of them, nine watts each. That is 72 watts. For 8 hours, that is 576 watt-hours. It fits. Just.'
'And the lift?' asked Mr. Pillai. 'The lift is twelve hundred watts. It only runs for a minute at a time.'

'Twelve hundred watts for just twenty minutes in all is four hundred watt-hours,' said Mini, working it out quickly. 'We do not have four hundred. And the pump is eight hundred watts. One hour of the pump is eight hundred watt-hours. That is more than all that is left.'
Mr. Pillai said nothing for a while. A grown-up who has made a plan does not like to hear that the plan does not add up. But he had also seen the numbers on the bill, in her small neat writing.
'The fan in my flat is only sixty watts,' said a neighbour. 'I will be too hot.'

'Sixty watts for eight hours is four hundred and eighty,' said Mini. 'That is also too much. But a wet cloth and a window is free.' She smiled. 'And here is the surprise. Your little fan uses more than the big kettle, if you leave it on all night. It is not how strong the thing is. It is how strong, and for how long.'

They switched off the lift. They switched off the pump. They switched on only the stair lights and Annamma Aunty's machine. In the dark corridor, the nine-watt bulbs glowed a soft yellow, and from the third floor came the quiet hum of the machine.

Mini sat on the stairs with Mr. Pillai and checked the number on the grey box every hour. At midnight, it said 2,250. At two in the morning, 1,500. 'Just as we planned,' she said. 'Our plan was three hundred and seventy-two watt-hours every hour. We are keeping to the plan.'

At a quarter past five, as the sky turned grey, the lights came back. The fans started turning. The pump started with a growl. The grey box still said 300 watt-hours, just what Mini's plan had promised.
Mr. Pillai looked at it for a long time. 'Tomorrow,' he said, 'you will come to the building meeting, Mini. I want you to explain this to everyone.'
'I will bring my pencil,' said Mini.
story.epiphany: A battery holds a fixed number of watt-hours. Divide that number by the watts of the things you run, and you get the hours. A small thing left on all night can use more than a big thing used for a few minutes.
ask: Why could the building not run the lift and the pump as well as the breathing machine?
Mini said a small fan can use more than a big kettle. When is that true?
A battery holds 3,000 watt-hours. How would you find how long it runs a 100 watt television?

games.title: Budget the Battery: plan a night without power
games.context: This is a planning game. A battery holds a fixed number of watt-hours, and each appliance uses watts times hours. You choose what to run so you keep the most important things going all night.

items.b: 800 watts times 1 hour is 800 watt-hours. That is 8 squares. Points: 5.

items.b: 500 watts times one fifth of an hour is 100 watt-hours. That is 1 square. Points: 2.

items.f: Electric kettle. 1,500 watts. Runs for 4 minutes, which is one fifteenth of an hour.
items.b: 1,500 watts times one fifteenth of an hour is 100 watt-hours. That is 1 square. Points: 1.
50 watts times 4 hours is 200 watt-hours. That is 2 squares. Points: 2.

items.f: Lift. 1,200 watts. Runs for 20 minutes in all, which is one third of an hour.
items.b: 1,200 watts times one third of an hour is 400 watt-hours. That is 4 squares. Points: 1.

items.f: Breathing machine for a neighbour. 300 watts. Runs for 8 hours.
items.b: 300 watts times 8 hours is 2,400 watt-hours. That is 24 squares. Points: 20.

items.f: Stair lights. Eight LED bulbs of 9 watts each. Run for 8 hours.
items.b: Eight bulbs of 9 watts is 72 watts. 72 watts times 8 hours is 576 watt-hours. That is 6 squares. Points: 3.

items.f: SURPRISE. The battery was not fully charged.
items.b: Cross out 3 squares of your battery. If your cards no longer fit, put back the card with the fewest points.

items.f: SURPRISE. A neighbour shares her battery.
items.b: Draw 2 more squares on your battery. You may add one more card if it fits.

items.f: SURPRISE. It is a very hot night.
items.b: The ceiling fan card is worth 3 more points. If you did not choose it, you may swap one card for it if it fits.

items.f: SURPRISE. The power cut lasts 2 hours longer than planned.
items.b: Cross out 4 squares of your battery. If your cards no longer fit, put back the card with the fewest points.

printables.title: Battery board: draw 30 squares in 3 rows of 10
items: Thirty squares is a battery of 3,000 watt-hours.
Cross out a square for every 100 watt-hours your cards use.

rules: Each player draws a battery of 30 squares. One square is 100 watt-hours. Put the 12 appliance cards face up, with the fronts showing. Keep the 4 surprise cards face down.
Each player works out the watt-hours for every appliance card, by multiplying watts by hours. Turn the card over to check. One point for each card you got right before turning it.

Now plan the night. Each player chooses cards to run, and crosses out squares for each. You may not use more than 30 squares. A card costs its squares in full, and each card can be used once by each player, so two players may choose the same card.
Then one player turns over a surprise card, and everyone follows it. If your plan no longer fits, put back the card with the fewest points.
Add up the points on your chosen cards, and the points for the sums you got right. The highest score wins.
Playing alone, try to beat 30 points, counting the points for your sums. Notice that the card with the most points also costs the most squares. Ask yourself if it is worth it.
With a parent, take turns. The parent tries to find a plan that scores better, and explains the sums.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 cards. Put the 12 appliance cards face up. Draw a battery of 30 squares for each player. One square is 100 watt-hours.
flow.say: This battery holds 3,000 watt-hours. A watt-hour is one watt used for one hour. We draw 30 squares, and each square is 100 watt-hours.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw a battery of 30 squares.
flow.parent: You need scissors, paper, a pencil and a calculator. With 2 to 4 players, each draws a battery and everyone plays at once from the same face-up cards. Check that your child can say what a watt-hour is. If not, say that a 10 watt bulb on for 1 hour uses 10 watt-hours.
flow.context: This is the first step of Budget the Battery. You set up the cards and the battery.

flow.do: Each player works out the watt-hours for every appliance card. Write the number under each card. Then turn the card over to check, and score one point for each right.
flow.say: Multiply watts by hours to get watt-hours. Then divide by 100 to get the squares. Do not turn the card over until you have your answer.
flow.kid: Multiply watts by hours. Write it down. Then check the back.
flow.parent: Let your child use a calculator. If a card uses minutes, change them to part of an hour first. 12 minutes is one fifth of an hour, and 4 minutes is one fifteenth. A wrong answer is a chance to ask what they multiplied.

check.q: A 100 watt television runs for 3 hours. How many watt-hours is that?
check.why: Watt-hours are watts times hours, and 100 times 3 is 300. Adding the numbers gives 103, which mixes up the two different things. Dividing gives 33, which is not what the question asks.

flow.context: In this step, you work out how many squares each appliance uses.

flow.do: Now plan the night. Choose the cards you will run, and cross out the squares. You may use up to 30 squares. Write down the points.
flow.say: Which things matter most tonight? Which cost too much? Choose your cards, and cross out the squares. Do not go over 30.
flow.kid: Choose cards. Cross out squares. Stay at 30 or under.

ask.q: Which card costs a lot but gives few points?

flow.parent: Let your child decide. The breathing machine is worth 20 points but takes 24 squares, so it leaves only 6. Ask what they would give up to keep it. There is no wrong plan, only plans with more or fewer points.
flow.context: In this step, you choose what to run with your battery.

flow.do: Turn over one surprise card. Everyone follows it. Change your plan if it no longer fits. Add up your points and say who won.
flow.say: A surprise is coming. Turn it over and follow it. Does your plan still fit? What will you give up?
flow.kid: Turn a surprise card. Follow it. Does your plan still fit?
flow.parent: A good plan is one that can survive a surprise. Ask your child to say what they gave up and why. After the game, say the idea: the battery holds a fixed amount, and the hours it lasts depend on the watts you run.
flow.context: In this step, you face a surprise and add up your points.

experiments.title: Stair Power: how many watts are you?
experiments.question: If you climb the same stairs slowly and then fast, does the fast climb use more energy, or only more watts?
experiments.predict: Before you climb, guess. Will the fast climb use more energy than the slow one? Will it use more watts? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same stairs, the same child and the same clothes are used for every climb. Nothing is carried. Only the speed changes: slow, steady and fast. Each speed is done twice, with two minutes of rest in between, so one odd climb does not fool you. The climb is always a walk, never a run.

materials.item: a staircase with a rail and at least 10 steps, with a grown-up at the top and the bottom (or one sturdy step about 20 centimetres high)
a phone or watch with a stopwatch, held by the grown-up
a ruler or tape measure
a bathroom scale, or use the mass given in step 2
a phone calculator
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Use dry stairs with a rail, and wear shoes or chappals with a good grip. Always walk, never run, and hold the rail. A grown-up stands at the top and the bottom. Rest two minutes between climbs, and stop at once if your child feels dizzy or very out of breath. Do the climbs when the stairs are quiet.
experiments.record: Fill in a row of the table for each climb. Then draw a bar chart of the watts for the six climbs, using the same scale for every bar.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you climb a staircase at three speeds and turn each climb into joules and watts.

setup.art: A child measuring the height of one stair step with a ruler while a parent holds the end.
setup.caption: 1. Measure one step with a ruler. Count the steps in the flight.

setup.art: A child standing on a bathroom scale with a number showing.
setup.caption: 2. Find your mass in kilograms, on a scale or from the step below.

setup.art: A child walking up a staircase holding the rail with a parent at the top holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. Climb at one speed while a grown-up times you from the first step to the last.

setup.art: A results table on paper with columns for steps, seconds, joules and watts and a pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Write the time in the table. Work out the joules and the watts.

setup.art: Three children's drawings of bars of different heights next to a bulb and a fan labelled 9 W and 60 W.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar for each climb. Compare it with a bulb and a fan.

flow.do: Show your child the stairs. Say they will climb three times: slowly, at a steady pace, and fast. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will climb these stairs three ways. Slowly, then steady, then fast. Will the fast climb use more energy than the slow one? Will it use more watts? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will climb three ways. Slow, steady and fast. Which uses more energy? Which uses more watts? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the fast climb will use more?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the fast climb uses more of everything. Write the guess and the reason at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stair Power. You guess before you climb.

flow.do: Measure the height of one step in centimetres. Count the steps in the flight. Multiply the two numbers, then divide by 100, to find the height of the climb in metres. Find your child's mass, or use 25 kilograms for a young child and 30 for an older one.
flow.say: First we need three numbers. How high is one step? How many steps are there? How heavy are you? We will use them to find the joules of every climb.
flow.kid: Measure one step. Count the steps. Find your mass in kilograms.
flow.parent: A typical step is 15 to 18 centimetres. Twenty steps of 17 centimetres is 3.4 metres. The energy to lift your body is the mass in kilograms, times 10, times the climb in metres. For 30 kilograms and 3.4 metres, that is 30 times 10 times 3.4, which is 1,020 joules. You work this out once. If there are no stairs, use one sturdy step about 20 centimetres high. Count each step up as 0.2 metres. Do 30 step-ups for one climb of 6 metres.

check.q: A child of 30 kilograms climbs 3 metres. About how many joules is that? Use 10 joules for lifting 1 kilogram by 1 metre.
check.why: 30 kilograms times 10 joules times 3 metres is 900 joules. If you picked 90, you used the mass but forgot the 10 joules per kilogram. Check the working again, one step at a time.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the stairs and your mass. You use them to find how many joules the climb takes.

flow.do: A grown-up stands at the top with the stopwatch. Your child climbs slowly, then rests for two minutes. Then your child climbs at a steady pace, rests, and climbs at a fast walk. Repeat all three climbs. Write each time in seconds.
flow.say: Walk up with one hand on the rail. Start the stopwatch on the first step. Stop it on the last. Never run. Rest for two minutes between climbs.
flow.kid: Hold the rail. Walk up at the speed we say. Rest two minutes each time.

ask.q: How do your legs feel after the fast climb, compared with the slow one?

flow.parent: A slow climb of 20 steps may take about 30 seconds. A steady climb may take 20 seconds. A fast walk may take 12 seconds. These are typical, and yours will differ. Keep the three speeds clearly different. Stand beside your child on the first climb so they are safe. Number the six climbs one to six in the table. With 2 to 4 children, take turns in four jobs: climber, timer, writer, and rail watcher. Each child climbs each speed once, and the others time. Each child rests while timing a sibling. Each child uses their own mass, so compare watts, not who is stronger. Do not race, and never let a child go faster than a quick walk.
flow.context: In this step, you climb the stairs six times and write down the time of each climb.

flow.do: For each climb, divide the joules by the seconds. That gives the watts. Fill in the table. Compare the joules in each row, then the watts.
flow.say: Power is energy divided by time. Take the joules of the climb and divide by the seconds it took. What do you get for the slow climb? And for the fast climb?
flow.kid: Divide the joules by the seconds. That gives the watts. Fill in the table.

ask.q: Which column changed from climb to climb, and which stayed nearly the same?
good: The seconds and the watts changed.
The climb was the same height.

flow.parent: If the climb is 1,020 joules, a 30 second climb is 34 watts. A 10 second climb is 102 watts. Check that the joules column is nearly the same in every row, because it is the same climb. Only the watts change. If the joules look different, the climb was not the same height. Check the step count.

check.q: A climb used 900 joules and took 10 seconds. How many watts did the child make?
check.why: Watts are joules divided by seconds, and 900 divided by 10 is 90. A 9 means you divided by 100. Check which numbers you divided.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the watts of each climb from the joules and the seconds.

flow.do: Draw a bar for the watts of each climb. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Compare their best climb with a 9 watt bulb and a 60 watt fan.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see in the table? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer says the joules stayed about the same, because the climb was the same height, and the watts were bigger when the time was shorter. After they have said this, say the idea: the same energy in less time is more power. Say too that the muscles use about four times the watts you measured, because they turn only a quarter of their food energy into lifting. The other three quarters become heat, which is why you feel hot. A quick walk up may give about 80 to 120 watts, more than a fan, but nobody can keep that up for hours.
flow.think: You made more watts than a bulb for a few seconds. Why can you not light a bulb all night this way?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the results and say what they show. You compare your power with a bulb and a fan.

experiments.title: Meter Blink: how many watts is each appliance?
experiments.question: Can the blinking light on the energy meter tell us how many watts each appliance takes, and does it match the rating plate?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which appliance will make the meter light blink fastest? Which will blink slowest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everything else in the home stays the same while you test one appliance. First you measure the home with the appliance off, and then with it on. The difference is the appliance alone. You use the same stopwatch and the same way of counting each time.

materials.item: your home's energy meter with a blinking light, and the number on it that says blinks per kilowatt-hour (usually written imp/kWh; common values are 1,600 and 3,200, but some meters differ, so use your own)
a phone stopwatch
a phone calculator
a ceiling fan, a medium appliance such as a TV or mixer grinder, and one heating appliance such as an iron, kettle or geyser, all used by a grown-up
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Only look at the meter. Never open the meter box or touch the wires. A grown-up switches the big appliance on and off, because irons and kettles get very hot. Do not leave the big appliance running longer than the count needs. Keep hands dry and away from plugs and sockets, keep the iron on its stand and never leave it alone, and keep fingers out of the mixer grinder.
experiments.record: Write each appliance, how you counted, the seconds, and the watts you worked out. Add the rating plate watts and say if they are close.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you use the blinking light on your energy meter to find how many watts each appliance takes.

setup.art: A white energy meter on a wall with a small red light blinking and the number 3200 imp/kWh printed on it.
setup.caption: 1. Find the blinking light. Read the number that says imp/kWh.

setup.art: A child holding a phone stopwatch and counting blinks on the meter while a parent holds a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Count the blinks for 120 seconds, or time 10 blinks.

setup.art: A ceiling fan switched on, with the meter light blinking faster in the next picture.
setup.caption: 3. Switch on one appliance and count again.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of appliances, blinks and watts, and a rating plate drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Work out the watts. Compare with the rating plate.

flow.do: List four appliances in your home. Ask your child to put them in order from the fastest blink to the slowest, and say why. Write down the order.
flow.say: When we switch something on, the light on the meter blinks. Which of these will make it blink fastest? Which slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the appliances in order. Fastest blink first. Say why.

ask.q: What makes you think that one will blink fastest?

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Many children say the biggest or loudest machine blinks fastest. Others pick the one used most. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Meter Blink. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Find the meter. If it is in a shared box, ask the building staff to show you. Read the number printed next to imp/kWh. It says how many blinks make one unit. Divide 3,600,000 by that number to find the joules in each blink.
flow.say: Each blink means the meter has counted a fixed amount of energy. The number on the meter says how many blinks make one unit. A unit is 3,600,000 joules. Divide to find the joules in one blink.
flow.kid: Find the blink number. Divide 3,600,000 by it. That is the joules in one blink.
flow.parent: Common numbers are 1,600 and 3,200 blinks per unit. At 3,200, each blink is 1,125 joules. At 1,600, each blink is 2,250 joules. Many flats have the meter in a common box, so ask a grown-up in the building to show you. Do not open it. Look from a safe distance, and do not lean into the box. If your meter has a spinning disc, it prints revolutions per unit instead. Count turns instead of blinks. If you cannot see the meter at all, do the Rating Plate Hunt instead.

check.q: A meter says 1,600 blinks per unit. A unit is 3,600,000 joules. How many joules is one blink?
check.why: 3,600,000 divided by 1,600 is 2,250. The meter counts a fixed amount of energy in every blink. If you picked 1,600, you used the blink number without dividing.

flow.context: In this step, you find the meter and work out how much energy one blink counts.

flow.do: Switch off everything you can. Keep the fridge on, because it must stay on. Count the blinks for 120 seconds, or time how long 10 blinks take. Write down the number and the seconds.
flow.say: First we measure the home with nothing extra on. Count every blink for two minutes. This is the background that we will take away later.
flow.kid: Count blinks for two minutes. This is the home with nothing extra on.

ask.q: Why do we measure the home before we switch anything on?
good: So we can take it away.
To see what the fridge uses.
So we only measure the new thing.

flow.parent: The fridge, a router and clocks always use a little. This is the base. The meter may blink slowly, at around one blink every 5 to 20 seconds. Count the base twice. If the two counts differ by more than 2 blinks, the fridge motor started or stopped, so repeat until they agree. Switch off the air conditioner and geyser for the test, but keep the fan you will test. Joules counted equals blinks times the joules in one blink. Watts equals joules divided by seconds.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the energy the home uses with nothing extra switched on.

flow.do: Switch on one appliance. For a slow blink, count blinks for 120 seconds. For a fast blink, time how long 10 blinks take. Switch it off. Do the fan, then the mixer grinder, then the iron.
flow.say: Now switch on the fan. Count the blinks for two minutes. Write it down. Then do the mixer grinder. A grown-up will do the iron, and time ten blinks.
flow.kid: Switch on one appliance. Count the blinks. Write the number. Switch it off.
flow.parent: Watts for each row equals blinks times the joules per blink, divided by the seconds. Then take away the base watts, which you measured with nothing extra switched on. Example at 3,200 blinks per unit: the base count was 11 blinks in 120 seconds, which is 12,375 joules, or about 103 watts. With the fan on, the count was 18 blinks, which is 20,250 joules, or about 169 watts. Take away the base and the fan is about 66 watts. A 1,000 watt iron blinks about once a second at 3,200 per unit. Let the grown-up time ten blinks, which takes about 11 seconds. Be honest about the size of the error: one blink is 1,125 joules, so over 120 seconds a single blink is about 9 watts. For an appliance with few watts, such as a fan, count for 300 seconds if you have time. A heating appliance such as an iron switches its heater on and off, so its average may be below its rating plate. With 2 to 4 children, one counts blinks aloud, one times, one writes, and the grown-up works the appliance. Swap jobs for each appliance.

check.q: At 3,200 blinks per unit, switching on a fan adds 7 blinks in 120 seconds to the base count. Each blink is 1,125 joules. About how many watts is that?
check.why: 7 blinks times 1,125 joules is 7,875 joules. Divided by 120 seconds that is about 65 watts. A fan is usually around 50 to 75 watts. If you picked 650, you may have divided by 12 instead of 120.

flow.context: In this step, you test each appliance and work out its watts.

flow.do: Find the rating plate on each appliance. Compare it with your watts. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Does your number match the rating plate? Tell me what you thought, what you saw, and why you think it came out that way.
flow.kid: Compare with the rating plate. Say what you thought and what you saw.
flow.parent: The numbers will not match exactly. The plate gives the most the appliance uses. A fan on a low speed uses less. A light with a dimmer uses less. If a result is far off, count again. After your child has spoken, say the idea: the meter counts energy for the whole home, and a blink is a fixed amount of energy. Faster blinks mean more watts. One LED bulb of 9 watts adds less than one blink in two minutes, so the meter cannot show it. That is a result too: a small appliance is hard to see among the blinks of big ones.
flow.think: If the meter blinks the same number of times on two different days, was the same energy used on both days?
flow.context: In this step, you compare your measured watts with the rating plate and say what the blinks showed.

activities.title: A Ladder of Lifts: how many joules is that?

materials.item: a 1 litre bottle of water, which has a mass of about 1 kilogram
an apple or a small fruit of about 100 grams
a table or shelf about 80 centimetres high, and a ruler or tape
a phone stopwatch and a calculator
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Lift an apple, then a bottle. Lift the bottle 20 times. Work out the joules and compare them with a chapati.

activities.record: Write the joules of one lift, the joules of twenty lifts, and how many lifts equal one chapati.
activities.safety: Close the bottle cap tightly. Lift with bent knees and a straight back, and put the bottle down gently. Keep your feet clear of the bottle. Stop if you feel tired or your back hurts.
activities.context: In this activity, you feel what a joule is by lifting an apple and a bottle. Then you compare your lifting with the energy in a chapati.

setup.art: A child lifting a small apple one metre up beside a ruler with 1 joule written beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lift an apple 1 metre. That is about 1 joule.

setup.art: A child lifting a 1 litre water bottle onto a table 80 centimetres high.
setup.caption: 2. Lift the bottle onto the table. Do it 20 times.

setup.art: A notebook with a sum showing 10 times 0.8 equals 8 joules for one lift and a chapati beside it labelled 420,000 joules.
setup.caption: 3. Work out the joules. Compare them with a chapati.

flow.do: Hold the apple. Lift it up from your hip to above your head, about one metre. Say that this small lift is about 1 joule. Ask what a bottle ten times heavier would need.
flow.say: This apple is about a tenth of a kilogram. Lifting it one metre takes about 1 joule. What do you think lifting the bottle one metre will take?
flow.kid: Lift the apple 1 metre. That is about 1 joule. How many joules for the bottle?

ask.q: How many apples weigh the same as the bottle?

flow.parent: The bottle is about 10 times heavier than the apple, so lifting it the same height takes about 10 times the energy, 10 joules. Let your child say this before you do.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ladder of Lifts. You feel one joule.

flow.do: First guess how many lifts you can do before you feel tired, and write it. Measure the table height in metres. Lift the bottle from the floor to the table, 20 times, at an easy pace. Your child counts each lift out loud and the grown-up times the 20 lifts.
flow.say: Lift the bottle onto the table, then put it back on the floor, and lift again. Count out loud. Stop if you get tired.
flow.kid: Lift the bottle onto the table. Count each lift. Do it 20 times.
flow.parent: Only the lifts up count as energy, not the lowering. A table 80 centimetres high is 0.8 metres. One lift is 10 joules times 0.8, which is 8 joules. Twenty lifts are 160 joules. Time them. Twenty lifts in 40 seconds is 4 watts of lifting, but your body used about four times that. With 2 to 4 children, each lifts 20 times while a sibling counts and another times. Compare the seconds: the joules are the same, so the child who was quicker made more watts. If your table is not about 80 centimetres, use its measured height.
flow.context: In this step, you lift a bottle 20 times and count.

flow.do: First ask: how many bottle lifts would equal the energy of one chapati? Write a guess and a reason. Then work it out. A chapati holds about 420,000 joules. Divide by 8 joules for one lift.
flow.say: A chapati holds about 420,000 joules. One bottle lift is 8 joules. How many lifts is one chapati? First guess, and tell me why. Then use the calculator.
flow.kid: How many lifts equal one chapati? Guess first. Then work it out.

ask.q: Why does eating one chapati not let you lift the bottle 52,500 times at once?
good: The body lets the energy out slowly.

flow.parent: The sum is 420,000 divided by 8, which is 52,500 lifts. Your child will probably guess far too low. Say that this number is only right if none of the chapati's energy is wasted. Your muscles use about four times what the lift needs, so in real life it is about 13,000 lifts. A chapati could keep you lifting for hours. The 420,000 joules is typical for one chapati of about 100 kilocalories, and real chapatis vary.

check.q: A chapati holds about 420,000 joules. Lifting the bottle once takes about 10 joules. About how many lifts is that?
check.why: 420,000 divided by 10 is 42,000. If you picked 420, you took away three zeros instead of one. The chapati holds a very large number of lifts.

flow.context: In this step, you work out how many lifts a chapati holds. You guess first.

activities.title: Rating Plate Hunt: the watts in our home

materials.item: eight appliances in the home, such as a fan, a light, a mixer grinder, an iron, a TV, a charger, a fridge and a geyser
a torch to read small labels
a phone calculator
paper with a table and a pencil

schedule.what: Find each rating plate, write the watts, guess the hours, and work out the energy for a day.

activities.record: A table with the appliance, its watts, the hours it runs in a day, the watt-hours, and the order from most to least.
activities.safety: Read the plates only on appliances that are switched off and cool. A grown-up reads the geyser plate and moves the heavy things. Stand on the floor, never on a chair. Do not pull plugs or open anything.
activities.context: In this activity, you find the watts on eight appliances and work out which one uses the most energy in a day.

setup.art: A child shining a torch at the label on the back of a mixer grinder.
setup.caption: 1. Find the rating plate on each appliance. Look for the letter W.

setup.art: A paper table with eight rows of appliances, watts and hours.
setup.caption: 2. Write the watts. Guess the hours it runs in a day.

setup.art: The same table with a column of watt-hours and a star beside the biggest number.
setup.caption: 3. Multiply watts by hours. Find the biggest user.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which of eight appliances uses the most energy in a day, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Here are eight things in our home. Which one will use the most energy in a whole day? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Eight appliances. Which uses the most energy in a day? Why?

ask.q: What makes you think that one uses the most?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children pick the biggest, loudest or hottest one. Others pick the one that is always on. Both ideas are good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rating Plate Hunt. You guess before you look.

flow.do: Find the rating plate on each appliance, usually on the back or the bottom. Read the watts. Do not open anything or pull a plug. Write the watts in the table. Some plates show volts and amps instead. Multiply them to get watts.
flow.say: Look for a label with the letter W. This is the power of the appliance. Read it to me, and write it in the table.
flow.kid: Find the label with a W. Read the number. Write it down.
flow.parent: A fan may say 60 or 75 W. An LED bulb says 9 W. A mixer grinder says 500 to 750 W. An iron says 1,000 W. A geyser says 2,000 W. A phone charger says 10 to 20 W. A fridge says 100 to 200 W. If a plate shows only volts and amps, multiply the two to get watts. For example, 230 volts times 0.5 amps is 115 watts. The fridge plate is often on the inside wall or the back, so look inside the door first and do not pull the fridge out. If you cannot find a plate, use the typical number given here and say so. With 2 to 4 children, give each child two appliances to read and write, then share the table.
flow.context: In this step, you find the watts of each appliance on its rating plate.

flow.do: For each appliance, guess the hours it runs in a day. Multiply watts by hours. Put the answers in order from most to least. Compare with the first guess.
flow.say: Now guess the hours each one runs in a day. Multiply watts by hours. Which one is biggest? Is it the one you guessed?
flow.kid: Guess the hours. Multiply watts by hours. Which is biggest?
flow.parent: A geyser of 2,000 watts for half an hour is 1,000 watt-hours. A fan of 60 watts for 12 hours is 720. A fridge of 150 watts running half the time over 24 hours is 1,800. Often the fridge or the air conditioner is the biggest. Your child may be surprised to find that the quiet fridge uses more than the loud mixer.

check.q: A 60 watt fan runs for 12 hours and a 2,000 watt geyser runs for 15 minutes. Which uses more energy?
options: The geyser, because it has more watts
The fan, because it runs much longer
check.why: The fan uses 60 times 12, which is 720 watt-hours. The geyser uses 2,000 times a quarter of an hour, which is 500 watt-hours. So the fan uses more. If you picked the geyser, you looked only at the watts. You must multiply, because time matters as much as watts.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the energy each appliance uses in a day.

activities.title: Litres and Litres a Minute: amount and rate

materials.item: a 1 litre bottle, and a bucket or sink
a tap that you can open a little or a lot
a phone stopwatch
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Fill the bottle slowly, then fast. Time each one. Work out litres a minute.

activities.record: Write the seconds to fill the bottle slowly and fast, and the litres a minute for each. Also write your prediction for the 20 litre bucket.
activities.context: In this activity, you fill the same bottle from a thin trickle and from a full tap, to see the difference between an amount and a rate. Joules are like litres, and watts are like litres a minute.

setup.art: A tap running a thin trickle into a one litre bottle with a child holding a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Open the tap a little. Time how long the bottle takes to fill.

setup.art: A tap running hard into the same bottle with the stopwatch showing a short time.
setup.caption: 2. Open the tap a lot. Time it again.

setup.art: A paper with the two times and the sum 60 divided by the seconds beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Work out litres a minute for each.

flow.do: Hold the bottle. Ask your child how long it will take to fill from a trickle, and from a full tap. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will fill this one litre bottle two ways. A thin trickle, and a full tap. How long will each take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill a bottle two ways. How long will each take? Why?

ask.q: How many times longer will the trickle take?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often say the trickle takes about twice as long. It may take ten or more times as long.
flow.context: This is the first step of Litres and Litres a Minute. You guess before you fill.

flow.do: Fill the bottle from a thin trickle and time it. Pour the water out. Fill it from a full tap and time it. Do each twice. Write the seconds.
flow.say: Open the tap just a little. Start the stopwatch. Stop when the bottle is full. Now open the tap wide, and do it again.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle from a trickle. Time it. Fill it from a full tap. Time it.

ask.q: The bottle held the same water both times. What was different?

flow.parent: A thin trickle may take 60 to 120 seconds. A full tap may take about 5 to 15 seconds, depending on the water pressure. Tell your child the amount is the same, one litre, but the rate is very different. If the tap is fast, fill over the sink. Pour the water into a bucket and use it for plants or mopping, so none is wasted. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the bottle, one works the tap, one times, one writes. Swap and repeat.
flow.context: In this step, you time the same bottle filling slowly and fast.

flow.do: Divide 60 by the seconds to get litres a minute. Do it for both. Say that watts work like litres a minute, and joules like litres. Then predict: how long would a 20 litre bucket take from the trickle, and from the full tap?
flow.say: Divide 60 by the seconds it took. That gives the litres in one minute. Do it for the trickle and the full tap. Joules are like the litres. Watts are like litres a minute.
flow.kid: Divide 60 by your seconds. That is litres a minute.
flow.parent: A 5 second fill is 12 litres a minute. A 100 second fill is 0.6 litres a minute. Both times, the amount was the same one litre. In the same way, 3,600 joules could be 1 watt for an hour, or 3,600 watts for one second. At 0.6 litres a minute, a 20 litre bucket would take over 30 minutes. At 12 litres a minute it takes under 2 minutes. Fill the bucket from the full tap to check the second prediction. This is the same idea as an appliance: the power sets how fast the energy is used.

check.q: A tap fills a one litre bottle in 5 seconds. How many litres a minute is that?
check.why: There are 60 seconds in a minute, and 60 divided by 5 is 12. The tap would fill 12 bottles in a minute. If you picked 300, you multiplied instead of dividing.

flow.context: In this step, you turn your times into litres a minute and link the idea to joules and watts.

activities.title: Where Does the Rest Go? Feel the warmth

materials.item: an LED bulb in a lamp, a phone charger with a phone charging on it, a laptop, and a table fan motor or a Wi-Fi router (a ceiling fan is too high to touch safely), all on for at least 10 minutes
your hand, for feeling warmth with its back
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess which thing will feel warmest. Feel each thing with the back of your hand, put them in order, and say where the warmth comes from.

activities.record: List the four things from warmest to coolest, and write where the warm energy came from. Write each warmth score from 0 to 5.
activities.safety: Use the back of your hand, about 5 centimetres away first. Touch only if it feels no warmer than a cup of tea you can hold. Never touch a bulb that has been on for a long time, or an iron, a kettle or a geyser. A grown-up does the touching. Never put fingers near fan blades or in a fan guard. Touch only the motor housing, with the fan switched off and the blades stopped.
activities.context: In this activity, you feel the warmth that machines give out, which is the energy that was not used for the job.

setup.art: A child's hand held flat 5 centimetres from a glowing lamp with an LED bulb.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the back of your hand near a bulb that has been on for ten minutes.

setup.art: The same child feeling the warm case of a phone charger and a laptop base.
setup.caption: 2. Feel the charger and the laptop in the same way.

setup.art: A list on paper from warmest to coolest with small drawings.
setup.caption: 3. Put the four things in order and write why they are warm.

flow.do: Name four things that have been on for ten minutes. Ask which will feel warmest, and why. Write the order.
flow.say: These four things have been working for ten minutes. Which will feel warmest? Which will be coolest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four things have been on. Which is warmest? Why?

ask.q: Why would a machine be warm if it is making light or sound or moving air?

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Many children expect the bulb to be hottest because it makes light. An LED bulb is cool for its brightness, but its base can be warm.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does the Rest Go. You guess before you feel.

flow.do: A grown-up checks that everything is safe. Hold the back of your hand 5 centimetres from each thing first. Then touch gently only if it feels no hotter than tea. Give each a warmth score from 0 (cool as the table) to 5 (as warm as tea). Write the order.
flow.say: Hold the back of your hand near each one. Then touch very gently with the grown-up. Which is warmest? Does the order match your guess?
flow.kid: Hold the back of your hand near each. Then touch gently. Which is warmest?
flow.parent: Chargers, laptops and fan motors are usually warm. A filament bulb would be too hot to touch, so only look at it. If nothing feels warm, the appliance may not have been on long enough. Switch it on for 10 minutes more. For a fair comparison, also feel a charger that is plugged in with no phone on it. It should be cooler than the one that is charging. With 2 to 4 children, each scores separately without talking, then compare scores. Different scores are normal, because warmth is hard to judge by hand.
flow.context: In this step, you feel how warm each machine is.

flow.do: Ask: the machine was meant to make light, sound or movement. Why is it warm too? Say where the warmth came from.
flow.say: That machine was not meant to make warmth. Where did the warmth come from? Where does it go next?
flow.kid: Why is it warm? Where does that warmth go next?
flow.parent: A strong answer says some of the energy that went in turned into heat on the way, and that the warmth spreads into the air around. It is not gone. It is the spread-out energy. Let your child say it first.

check.q: A phone charger is warm. What does that tell you?
options: Some of the energy it takes in becomes heat instead of charging the phone
check.why: Every machine turns some of its energy into heat, so not all of the energy does the job. A charger that is a little warm is normal. It is broken only if it gets very hot or smells.

flow.context: In this step, you say where the warmth comes from and where it goes.

projects.title: The Bill Detective: where does our electricity go?

materials.item: your latest electricity bill, or a photo of it
a phone calculator
paper and a pencil
your results from the Rating Plate Hunt, if you did it

schedule.what: Read the bill. Find the units used and the days. Work out units a day and units a person.
Read the meter total at the same time on day 1 and day 2, and subtract. Skip this if the meter is out of reach.
Turn units into chapatis. List the three biggest users and pick one change.

projects.record: Write the units used, the days, the units a day and a person, the chapatis, and the three biggest users with one change.
projects.context: In this project, you read your family's electricity bill like a detective and turn the units into chapatis, to compare electricity with food.

setup.art: A child reading an electricity bill at a table with a pencil and calculator, with the word units circled.
setup.caption: 1. Find the units used and the days on the bill.

setup.art: A paper with sums: units divided by days, and divided by the people in the home.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the units a day and a person.

setup.art: A plate of nine chapatis next to a drawing of one electricity unit.
setup.caption: 3. Turn units into chapatis: one unit is about nine chapatis.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many units of electricity your home uses in one day. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: A unit on the bill is 3.6 million joules. How many units do you think our home uses in a day? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many units do we use in a day? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A flat of four people often uses about 4 to 10 units a day, but air conditioning can double that.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bill Detective. You guess before you read the bill.

flow.do: Find the units used and the number of days on the bill. Divide the units by the days. Then divide by the number of people in the home. Write both answers.
flow.say: Look for the word units, or kilowatt-hours. Find how many days the bill covers. Divide units by days. Then divide by how many of us live here.
flow.kid: Find the units and the days. Divide to find units a day.

ask.q: Which appliances do you think use most of those units?
good: The fan or the air conditioner.

flow.parent: A bill for 240 units over 30 days is 8 units a day. For four people, that is 2 units each. Some bills show tiers, with the first units cheaper. Ignore the money for now. If you cannot find the bill, use these made-up numbers and say so.

check.q: A bill shows 240 units used over 30 days. How many units a day is that?
check.why: 240 divided by 30 is 8. Twenty-four means you divided by 10. Two hundred seventy means you added the days instead of dividing.

flow.context: In this step, you find the units your home uses in a day and for each person.

flow.do: On day 1, if your meter shows the total units (kWh) on its screen or when you press a button, write the number and the time. On day 2, at the same time, read it again and subtract. That is the units for one day. Write it down.
flow.say: Let us check the sum on another day. Did we use about the same units today? Why might it change?
flow.kid: Check one more day. Did we use the same?
flow.parent: Meters in many flats are out of reach, and some prepaid meters show units only in an app. If you cannot read it, skip this step and use the bill's number. Days with a geyser, a guest or an air conditioner use more.
flow.context: In this step, you check your sum on another day.

flow.do: Turn the units a day into chapatis. One unit is about nine chapatis of 100 kilocalories each. Compare it with the food a person eats, about 20 chapatis a day. Name the three biggest users and choose one change.
flow.say: One unit is the food energy of about nine chapatis. So how many chapatis of electricity does each of us use in a day? Compare it with the chapatis we eat.
flow.kid: One unit is about 9 chapatis. How many chapatis of electricity a day?
flow.parent: At 2 units a person, that is about 18 chapatis of electricity a day, nearly as much as the food a person eats. Many children are surprised. Say that this is one family's number, not a rule. The three biggest users often include the fridge, the fan or air conditioner, and the geyser or iron. The change can be small, like switching off a light. If you did not do the Rating Plate Hunt, use the typical watts from that activity. With 2 to 4 children, one reads the bill, one divides, one turns units into chapatis, and each picks a change. Nine chapatis for a unit is rounded from about 8.6.
flow.think: Why do you think a person's electricity can be as much energy as their food?
flow.context: In this step, you turn units into chapatis and pick one change for the family.

projects.safety: Only look at the meter. Never open the meter box or touch wires. Keep the bill private and do not share its numbers online.

challenges.title: The Energy Ladder: ten rungs, each ten times bigger
challenges.problem: Build a ladder of energy on a wall or a long strip of paper. The bottom rung is 1 joule, and every rung above is exactly ten times bigger. For each rung, find or draw a real thing that holds about that much energy.
constraints: The bottom rung is 1 joule (lifting an apple 1 metre).
Each rung is exactly ten times the one below.
You need at least 9 rungs, up to 100 million joules.
Every rung needs a real thing, with a number you worked out or looked up, and where you got it.
materials: a long strip of paper, or sticky notes on a wall
your results from the stairs, the lifts and the bill
general: Use things from this unit: an apple lift, a bottle lift, a cell, a phone battery, a chapati, an electricity unit and a litre of petrol.
Put your stair climb on the ladder, at the rung nearest to your joules.
Write the number of zeros beside each rung.
creative: Draw each rung as a rung of a real ladder against a house wall, so the ladder climbs from a pebble to a petrol tanker.
Add a second ladder beside it for watts, from a phone charger to the whole Sun.
Add the energy of something nobody has measured at home, such as a lightning flash or a small earthquake, and say where you found it.
challenges.your_turn: Build your ladder with the rungs you choose. Which rung was hardest to fill? Which was the biggest surprise? Add one thing of your own that is not in this unit.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the size of energy. You build a ladder that shows how much energy things hold, from one joule to a hundred million.

setup.art: A long sheet of paper on a wall with ten rungs drawn, the lowest labelled 1 J and the next 10 J.
setup.caption: 1. Draw ten rungs. Label the bottom one 1 joule.

setup.art: A child writing a real thing next to each rung, such as a bottle at 10 joules and a phone battery at 60 kilojoules.
setup.caption: 2. Find a real thing for each rung and write it beside the rung.

setup.art: A finished ladder with a star where the child's own stair climb sits.
setup.caption: 3. Mark where your stair climb sits on the ladder.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Draw a ladder of ten rungs on a long strip of paper. Write 1 joule on the lowest rung and an apple lift beside it.
flow.say: We will build a ladder. Each rung is ten times bigger than the one below. The bottom rung is one joule. What is the next rung?
flow.kid: Draw ten rungs. Write 1 joule at the bottom.

ask.q: What number is the third rung?

flow.parent: Write the rungs as 1, 10, 100, 1,000, and so on. Count the zeros. Explain that one kilojoule is 1,000 joules and one megajoule is 1,000,000.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Energy Ladder. You set up the rungs.

flow.do: Find a real thing for each rung. Some are in this unit. Others you must work out or look up. A bottle lift is 10 joules. A cell is about 10 kilojoules. Write each beside its rung.
flow.say: Find something real for each rung. Lifting a bottle is about 10 joules. A small cell is about 10 kilojoules. A chapati is about 0.4 megajoule, so two or three make 1 megajoule. What else can you find?
flow.kid: Find a real thing for each rung. Write it beside the rung.
flow.parent: Helpful rungs: 1 J is an apple lift. 10 J is a bottle lift. 100 J is lifting a 10 kilogram bag of rice 1 metre. 1 kJ is 100 bottle lifts. 10 kJ is about an AA cell. 100 kJ is about two phone batteries. 1 MJ is about two and a half chapatis. 10 MJ is about a day of food for a grown-up. 100 MJ is about three litres of petrol. Treat the figures as rough. A tenth rung of 1,000 megajoules is about 30 litres of petrol. Look up what you cannot work out, with a grown-up, and say where you found it. With 2 to 4 children, give each child some rungs, then join the strips. Use sticky notes or paper, not tape on a painted wall.
flow.context: In this step, you fill each rung with a real thing and its energy.

flow.do: Mark where your stair climb sits on the ladder. Ask your child to find the biggest gap on the ladder and the biggest surprise.
flow.say: Where does your stair climb sit on the ladder? What surprised you most? Which rung has the thing you did not expect?
flow.kid: Mark your stair climb. What surprised you most?
flow.parent: A climb of about 1,000 joules sits at the 1 kilojoule rung. Many children are surprised that a whole electricity unit is nine chapatis. Ask them to say it in their own words.
flow.context: In this step, you place your own result on the ladder and say what surprised you.

flow.do: Change one thing and try again. Move one thing to a better rung, or add a second ladder for watts. Say why you moved it.
flow.say: Which thing is on the wrong rung? Which could you check better? Change one, and say why.
flow.kid: Fix one rung. Say why you changed it.
flow.parent: A good change comes from checking a number, not from guessing. Accept any change with a reason.
flow.context: In this step, you improve one rung of your ladder.
