videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

videos.title: Feynman's Building Blocks of Thermodynamics - with Andrea Sella
videos.why: For the parent and older children: a physicist explaining that energy is a number that stays the same.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

quiz.p: Which is the best description of a watt?
opts: One joule of energy every second
The amount of energy in a battery
quiz.why: A watt is a rate. One watt is one joule moving each second. The amount in a battery is counted in joules or watt-hours.

quiz.p: Which holds more energy, a chapati or a phone battery?
opts: A chapati holds about seven times as much
quiz.why: A chapati holds about 420 kilojoules and a phone battery about 60. A battery gives its energy out faster, but the chapati holds more.

quiz.p: A 1,000 watt iron runs for 30 minutes. A 100 watt television runs for 8 hours. Which uses more energy?
opts: The iron, because it has more watts
quiz.why: The iron uses 1,000 times half an hour, which is 500 watt-hours. The television uses 100 times 8, which is 800 watt-hours. Time matters as much as watts.

quiz.p: A child climbs the same stairs slowly, and then fast. What stays the same?
quiz.why: The climb is the same height and the same body, so the joules are the same. The seconds and the watts change.

quiz.p: A bulb is warm after an hour. What does the warmth show?
opts: Some of the energy it took in did not become light, and spread out as heat
The bulb is making new energy
quiz.why: Every bulb turns some energy into heat. The warmth is the spread-out energy. No machine makes new energy.

opts: Energy is never made or destroyed, only moved or changed
Energy is used up when a battery goes flat
Energy is made when a fire burns
quiz.why: A flat battery has given its energy to light, movement, sound and warmth. A fire changes stored energy into heat and light. The total stays the same.

quiz.p: The meter light blinks faster when a geyser is switched on. What does that mean?
opts: The home is taking energy at a higher rate, so more watts
quiz.why: Each blink counts the same amount of energy. More blinks each second means more energy each second, which is more watts.

quiz.p: What is one unit of electricity on a bill?
opts: 3.6 million joules, the energy of a 1,000 watt appliance running for an hour
quiz.why: One unit is one kilowatt-hour. That is 1,000 watts for 3,600 seconds, which is 3.6 million joules.

quiz.p: Burned on a plate, a chapati would let out its energy in a few minutes. Your body lets it out over about an hour at 100 watts. What does this show?
opts: The same joules can come out at very different watts
The body makes less energy than fire
A fire holds more energy than a body
quiz.why: The chapati holds the same joules either way. Only the speed of letting them out is different, and that speed is the power.

quiz.p: James Joule let a falling weight turn a paddle wheel in water. The same fall warmed the water by the same amount every time. What did this show?
opts: Movement can turn into heat at a fixed rate, so heat is not just a fluid that flows
Heat is a fluid that is poured into water
quiz.why: A fluid that only flows could not be made from movement. A fixed rate shows that movement and heat can be counted in the same unit.

quiz.p: At noon on a clear day, about how much sunlight power reaches one square metre of ground?
quiz.why: About 1,000 watts, which is like a 1,000 watt heater on every square metre. The Sun is very powerful, and the light is spread over a huge area.

quiz.p: A bigger watt rating always means a bigger electricity bill.
quiz.why: False. The bill depends on watts times hours. A small appliance on for a long time can cost more than a big one used briefly.

items.p: Which of these is a unit for counting how much energy there is?
items.why: The joule counts how much energy there is. The watt counts how fast energy moves. A metre counts length.

items.p: Which of these is a unit for how fast energy moves?
items.why: One watt means one joule every second. So the watt tells you the speed of the energy, not the amount.

items.p: A bulb of 9 watts takes 9 joules from the wall every second.
items.why: True. One watt is one joule every second, so 9 watts is 9 joules every second.

items.p: One watt means one ____ every second.
items.why: A watt is a rate. It is one joule of energy moving each second.

items.p: A ceiling fan of 60 watts runs for 5 hours. How many watt-hours does it use?
items.why: Watt-hours are watts times hours, and 60 times 5 is 300. Adding gives 65, which mixes up the two kinds of number. Dividing gives 12, which is not the question.

items.p: A mixer grinder of 500 watts runs for 6 minutes. Six minutes is one tenth of an hour. How many watt-hours does it use?
items.why: 500 watts times one tenth of an hour is 50 watt-hours. A short time keeps the energy small, even for a powerful machine.

items.p: Sort each thing by the main form of energy it is showing.
items: a glowing ember in a chulha
items.why: A moving thing shows movement energy. Hot things show heat. A beam shows light and a bell shows sound. Food and a stretched band hold stored energy that waits to be let out.

items.p: Match each thing to about how much energy it holds or needs.
items.why: Each bigger thing needs more energy. A bottle is ten times as heavy as an apple, so it needs ten times the energy. A chapati holds thousands of times more, and one unit of electricity is about nine chapatis.

items.p: Energy is used up when a battery goes flat.
items.why: False. The battery's energy went into light, movement, sound and warmth. It is still there, but spread out and too thin to use.

items.p: A 9 watt LED bulb and a 60 watt old bulb give the same light. Where does the extra energy of the old bulb go?
opts: Into warmth, which spreads into the air
It is used up and vanishes
Into extra light we cannot see
items.why: The old bulb turns only a few joules in every hundred into light. The rest becomes warmth in the bulb and the air. Energy does not vanish.

items.p: A kilojoule is ____ joules.
items.why: Kilo means a thousand. So a kilojoule is 1,000 joules.

items.p: A child of 30 kilograms climbs up 3 metres. Lifting 1 kilogram by 1 metre takes about 10 joules. How many joules does the climb take?
items.why: 30 times 10 times 3 is 900 joules. Mass, the 10 joules for every kilogram and metre, and the height all multiply.

items.p: In your own words, say the difference between a joule and a watt. Use filling a bucket as your example.
items.a: A joule is an amount, like the litres of water in the bucket. A watt is a rate, like litres every minute from the tap. The same bucket can fill slowly or fast.
items.why: A strong answer says a joule is how much, a watt is how fast, and uses water to show the difference.

items.p: A friend says, 'A bigger machine always uses more energy.' Give one example that shows she is wrong.
items.a: A 1,500 watt kettle used for 4 minutes uses less than a 60 watt fan left on for 10 hours. Time matters as much as watts.
items.why: A strong answer gives a small machine used for a long time, and a big one used briefly, with numbers.

items.p: Draw an LED bulb with two arrows, one for the useful energy and one for the spread-out energy. Make the arrows the right sizes.
items.a: A bulb with a big arrow labelled light and a smaller arrow labelled warmth.
items.why: For an LED bulb, more energy becomes light than becomes warmth, so the light arrow is the bigger one. For an old bulb, the warmth arrow would be bigger.

items.p: Why does the meter light blink faster when you switch on a geyser?
opts: The geyser takes more joules every second, so the meter counts more blinks every second
The geyser uses up the energy, so the meter has to hurry
The geyser makes the electricity hotter
items.why: Each blink counts the same fixed amount of energy. A geyser takes energy at a high rate in watts, so blinks come more often.

items.p: Put these steps in order for finding the watts of a stair climb.
a: Measure the steps and your mass
Work out the joules of the climb
Time the climb with a stopwatch
Divide the joules by the seconds
items.why: You need the joules of the climb first, then the seconds it took. Dividing the joules by the seconds gives the watts.

items.p: Two children have the same mass and climb the same stairs. The first child takes 20 seconds and the second child takes 10 seconds. Which is true?
opts: Both used the same joules, and the second child made twice the watts
The second child used twice the joules and the same watts
The first child made twice the watts
items.why: The climb is the same height, so the joules are the same. The second child did it in half the time, so that child's watts are twice as big.

items.p: A child of 30 kilograms climbs 3 metres in 12 seconds. The climb takes 900 joules. How many watts did she make?
items.why: 900 divided by 12 is 75. Power is energy divided by time.

items.p: A phone battery holds about 60 kilojoules and a chapati about 420 kilojoules. How many phone batteries is one chapati?
items.why: 420 divided by 60 is 7. The chapati holds seven times the energy.

items.p: A chapati holds the energy of seven phone batteries, yet it cannot charge a phone. Say why in two or three sentences.
items.a: The chapati's energy is stored in the way its atoms are joined, not as electricity. A body has to change it step by step into forms it can use, and it lets it out slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says that the form of the energy matters as well as the amount, and that a body lets its energy out slowly.

items.p: A 1,000 watt iron is on for 90 minutes. How many units, or kilowatt-hours, is that?
items.why: 90 minutes is 1.5 hours. 1 kilowatt times 1.5 hours is 1.5 kilowatt-hours.

items.p: A home uses 6 units in a day. About how many chapatis of energy is that? One unit is about 9 chapatis.
items.why: 6 times 9 is 54. If you picked 6, that is the units, not the chapatis. If you picked 540, you added one zero too many.

items.p: The energy an appliance uses equals its power times its ____.
items.why: Energy is power multiplied by the time it runs. A longer time means more energy.

items.p: Sort each statement by what it describes.
items: A fan takes 60 joules each second
Sunlight at noon brings 1,000 joules each second onto a square metre
A kettle takes 1,500 joules every second
items.why: An amount says how much in all. A rate says how much each second. Words like 'each second' or 'every second' are clues for a rate.

items.p: Two children are talking about a fan of 30 watts that runs all night.

views.says: It is only 30 watts. It costs almost nothing, so I will leave it on.
Small watts add up over many hours. I will switch it off when nobody is in the room.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you work out to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and works out the watt-hours, for example 30 watts times 10 hours is 300 watt-hours, then compares that with other things in the home.
items.why: Both have a point. A small appliance uses little each second, but time multiplies it. The only way to decide is to calculate watts times hours.

items.p: Your body uses about 100 watts. A chapati holds about 420,000 joules. For how many minutes could it keep you going at 100 watts?
items.why: 420,000 divided by 100 is 4,200 seconds. Divided by 60 that is 70 minutes. A whole day needs about twenty chapatis.

items.p: A ball rolls across the floor and stops. What happened to its movement energy?
opts: It became a little warmth and sound in the ball, the floor and the air
It went back to the Sun
items.why: Energy is never destroyed. Friction turned the movement into warmth and sound, and they spread out.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Joule, kilojoule, watt-hour, watt.
items.a: The watt, because it counts how fast energy moves. The other three count how much energy there is.
items.why: Joules, kilojoules and watt-hours are all amounts. The watt is a rate.

items.p: The fast stair climb used more joules than the slow climb.
items.why: False. The climb was the same height and the same body, so the joules were the same. The fast climb used more watts, because it took less time.

items.p: Draw two bars: one for a slow climb of 34 watts and one for a fast climb of 102 watts. Label each bar.
items.a: Two bars, with the fast bar three times as tall as the slow bar.
items.why: 102 divided by 34 is 3. The fast bar is three times as tall.

items.p: Joule dropped a weight to turn a paddle in water, and the water warmed. Why did this show that heat is not a fluid that can only flow from place to place?
items.a: The movement of the weight turned into heat. A fluid that only flows could not be made out of movement. So heat can be made, and it is a form of energy.
items.why: A strong answer says heat was made from movement, which a fluid that only flows could not be.

items.p: An appliance has a rating plate that says 230 volts and 2 amps. Watts are volts times amps. How many watts is it?
items.why: 230 times 2 is 460 watts. Volts times amps gives watts.

items.p: An appliance of 460 watts runs for 5 hours. How many units of electricity is that?
items.why: 460 times 5 is 2,300 watt-hours. Divided by 1,000 that is 2.3 units.

items.p: Heater A uses 2,000 watts for 1 hour. Heater B uses 1,000 watts for 2 hours. Which uses more energy?
items.why: 2,000 times 1 is 2,000. 1,000 times 2 is also 2,000. The bigger watts and the longer time cancel out.

items.p: A battery holds 3,000 watt-hours. A 100 watt television is the only thing running. For how many hours does the battery last?
items.why: 3,000 divided by 100 is 30 hours. Hours equal watt-hours divided by watts.

items.p: A family changed all their bulbs to LED, but their bill hardly changed. Give two reasons this could be true.
items.a: Bulbs may have been a small part of the bill, and the geyser, fridge or fan may use much more. The bulbs may also have been on for only a few hours a day.
items.why: A strong answer names two reasons using watts and hours, such as bulbs using little compared with a geyser or an air conditioner.

items.p: Two children are deciding whether to buy an LED bulb that costs more now but uses less energy.

views.says: Buy it. It uses less energy every night, so it saves money over a year.
Do not buy it. It costs more now, and our old bulb still works.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you work out to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and works out the units each bulb uses in a year and the cost of each, then compares.
items.why: The choice depends on how many hours the bulb is on. The more hours, the faster the saving. A calculation shows which is right.

items.p: Why do we say energy is 'spread out' rather than 'lost' when a ball stops bouncing?
opts: The warmth and sound it made are real energy, but too thin to use again
The ball still has all its energy
items.why: The energy is still there as warmth in the floor, the ball and the air. It is spread out so thin that we cannot gather it to do a job.

items.p: Put these in order of how much energy, from smallest to biggest.
items.why: An apple lift is about 1 joule. A phone battery is about 60 kilojoules. A chapati is about 420 kilojoules. A unit of electricity is about 3,600 kilojoules.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Kettle, iron, geyser, LED bulb.
items.a: The LED bulb, because its job is to give light. The other three are made to turn electrical energy into heat.
items.why: Heat is the useful energy for a kettle, an iron and a geyser. For an LED bulb, light is the useful energy and heat is the spread-out energy.

items.p: A solar panel of 2 square metres turns one fifth of the sunlight on it into electricity. Noon sunlight is about 1,000 watts on each square metre. How many watts does the panel give?
items.why: 2 square metres times 1,000 is 2,000 watts of sunlight. One fifth of 2,000 is 400 watts.

items.p: A solar panel gives 400 watts for 5 sunny hours. How many units is that?
items.why: 400 times 5 is 2,000 watt-hours. Divided by 1,000 that is 2 units.

items.p: Explain why the energy number on a food label may not be exactly the energy a body gets.
items.a: Labels use average values. How the food is cooked and chewed, and the tiny living beings in the gut, change how much a body gets. So two people can get different amounts.
items.why: A strong answer says labels are averages and names at least one thing, such as cooking or gut bacteria, that changes the amount.

items.p: Draw an energy chain for you climbing the stairs, from sunlight to the warmth you give to the air.
items.a: Sunlight, then a plant, then the food, then the muscles, then movement and warmth in the air, joined by arrows.
items.why: Each step passes the energy on. At the end, most becomes warmth in the air.

items.p: A fridge takes 150 watts for 12 hours each day, because its motor runs about half the time. How many units does it use in 30 days?
items.why: 150 times 12 is 1,800 watt-hours a day. Times 30 is 54,000 watt-hours. Divided by 1,000 that is 54 units.

items.p: Who should decide how much electricity a family 'needs'? Give one reason for your answer.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer gives a reason, for example that needs differ for a family with a person who needs a machine to breathe, or that everyone should be able to run a fan and a light.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives a reason that comes from what electricity is used for.

items.p: The same 3,600 joules could be 1 watt for an hour, or 3,600 watts for one second.
items.why: True. 1 watt times 3,600 seconds is 3,600 joules. 3,600 watts times 1 second is also 3,600 joules. The amount is the same. The rate is different.

open_questions.q: What is energy, underneath the numbers?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can count it exactly and it always adds up. Nobody can say what it is made of, or why the total never changes.

open_questions.q: Why does the total energy of the universe stay the same?
open_questions.why_open: One idea links it to the laws of nature working the same on every day. Nobody has shown why the laws are like that.

open_questions.q: Is the total energy of the whole universe exactly zero?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists think the pull of gravity counts as negative energy and cancels everything else. It is an idea, and nobody has shown it is true.

open_questions.q: Can we ever store the Sun's energy cheaply enough to use all night, for everyone?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries are improving but cost a lot. Scientists are testing new ways to store energy, and nobody knows which will win.

open_questions.q: How much of the energy in food does each body actually get?
open_questions.why_open: Labels show averages. Cooking, chewing and the tiny living beings in the gut change the amount, and scientists are still measuring how much.

maths.problem: A child of 30 kilograms climbs 18 steps in the Stair Power test, and each step is 17 centimetres high. The climb is 306 centimetres, or 3.06 metres. Using 10 joules for each kilogram and metre, how many joules is the climb? Round to the nearest ten.
maths.explain: 30 times 10 is 300. 300 times 3.06 is 918. Rounded to the nearest ten that is 920 joules.
maths.context: In the Stair Power test, you climb a staircase and turn the climb into joules and watts.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying mass, height and 10 turns a climb into a number of joules, so you can compare it with other things.

maths.problem: A child's climb up the stairs takes 918 joules and 9 seconds. How many watts did the child make?
maths.explain: Watts are joules divided by seconds. 918 divided by 9 is 102. So she made 102 watts for those 9 seconds.
maths.context: In the Stair Power test, you divide the joules by the seconds to find the watts.
maths.why_maths: Dividing joules by seconds tells how fast the energy was used, and that is the only way to compare a fast climb with a slow one.

maths.problem: The bar chart shows made-up watts for three climbs. How many more watts did the fast climb make than the slow climb?
maths.explain: The fast bar is 102 watts and the slow bar is 31 watts. 102 take away 31 is 71.
maths.context: In the Stair Power test, a child climbed the stairs slowly, at a steady pace and fast. The chart shows made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance how the watts grow with speed, and the difference between two bars tells you by how much.

maths.problem: A 9 watt LED bulb gives about the same light as a 60 watt filament bulb. About how many times as many watts does the filament bulb use? Round to the nearest whole number.
maths.explain: 60 divided by 9 is about 6.7. Rounded to the nearest whole number that is 7. So for every watt of the LED, the old bulb uses about 7 watts.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells how many times more energy one machine needs for the same job, which shows how efficient it is.

maths.problem: A 60 watt fan runs from 9 o'clock at night to 6 o'clock in the morning. How many hours is that, and how many watt-hours does it use?
maths.explain: From 9 at night to 6 in the morning is 3 hours to midnight and 6 more hours, which is 9 hours. 60 times 9 is 540 watt-hours.
maths.why_maths: To find the energy a night uses, you first need the exact length of the night, and then multiply by the watts.

maths.problem: One unit of electricity is 3,600,000 joules. How many kilojoules is that?
maths.explain: A kilojoule is 1,000 joules. 3,600,000 divided by 1,000 is 3,600. So one unit is 3,600 kilojoules.
maths.why_maths: Energy numbers get very big. Changing to kilojoules makes them smaller and easier to compare with a chapati's 420.

maths.problem: For this question only, suppose that an LED bulb turns 20 of every 100 joules into light, and a filament bulb turns 4 of every 100. What percent of its energy does each turn into light? How many times better is the LED?
maths.answer: 20 percent and 4 percent. The LED is 5 times better.
maths.explain: 20 out of 100 is 20 percent. 4 out of 100 is 4 percent. 20 divided by 4 is 5.
maths.why_maths: A percentage tells the useful share of the energy, so you can compare two machines that use different amounts.

maths.problem: In the Energy Ladder, the bottom rung is 1 joule and each rung is ten times the one below. How many joules is the 7th rung?
maths.explain: Rung 1 is 1, rung 2 is 10, rung 3 is 100, rung 4 is 1,000, rung 5 is 10,000, rung 6 is 100,000 and rung 7 is 1,000,000. Each step adds a zero.
maths.context: In the Energy Ladder challenge, you build a ladder where each rung is ten times bigger than the one below.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern of adding a zero lets you jump straight to any rung without writing every step.

roots.context: We have counted energy in joules and watts, on a staircase and on a meter. Now we ask what these numbers tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A chapati holds the energy of about seven phone batteries. Your body lets it out at about 100 watts, a trickle that lasts all day. How much energy something holds and how fast it comes out are two separate facts. Life lasts because energy comes out slowly.
deep_truth.habit: We say a thing is strong or full of energy as if energy had one size. But the amount (joules) and the speed (watts) are different, and a lot of energy let out all at once is a different thing from the same energy let out slowly.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Stair Power experiment, the same climb used the same joules whether you went slowly or fast, but the watts were very different. A chapati holds a large amount of energy, yet your body lets it out at only about 100 watts through the day.

three.who_am_i: Your body works like a slow fire of about 100 watts. It burns food all day to keep you warm and moving. It holds a large amount of energy and lets it out gently.
three.what_is_life: A body spends energy in tiny steps in every cell, steady and slow. That pace is part of what keeps a living being going, hour after hour.
three.what_is_this_world: The Sun sends about 1,000 watts onto each square metre at noon, and nearly everything on Earth runs on a small share of it.

roots.thread: Everything we measured had a number, and the numbers linked things that look different: a chapati, a phone battery, a staircase climb, a fan, the Sun. They all have energy, counted in the same unit. The total never changes. Only the form and the pace change. In a seed, a flame and a bulb it is the same energy, moving at different speeds. So the many things around us are one energy in different forms, moving at different paces.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing away what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Water is a small power working for a very long time. A slow trickle can wear away a rock, because energy is power times time.

teachings.teaching: Never treat a small good as nothing. A water pot is filled by drops of water falling, one by one.
teachings.link: Many small watts, left on for many hours, add up to a big number of joules, just like drops filling a pot.

teachings.source: Richard Feynman, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume 1, chapter 4
teachings.teaching: Energy is a number that stays the same through all the changes that happen in nature. Feynman said we have no knowledge of what energy is.
teachings.link: We counted energy on a staircase and on a meter, and it added up. Yet nobody knows what energy is underneath.

science.text: Mass is a store of energy. Einstein's equation E = mc² says that even a very small mass holds a huge amount of energy. One gram of mass holds about 90 million million joules.
Nobody knows what energy is underneath, or why its total never changes. One idea links it to the laws of nature working the same on every day.

other_view.view: Energy is only a number that physics keeps the same, a way of keeping the accounts. It has no awareness and no oneness. The pattern we find is in our sums, and nothing more needs to be added to explain it.

how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1800s, most scientists thought heat was an invisible fluid called caloric. It flowed from hot things to cold ones, and it could not be made or destroyed. James Prescott Joule was the son of a brewer in Salford, England, and he was not a university professor. In the 1840s he built a paddle wheel in a tub of water. A falling weight turned the wheel, and the water slowly warmed. He could read his thermometer to a fraction of a degree. He found that the same amount of falling always gave the same warming. If heat were a fluid, turning a paddle would not make more of it. So movement had turned into heat, at a fixed rate. Joule reported this in 1850. The unit of energy is named after him.
how_we_found_out.who: James Prescott Joule, a brewer and amateur scientist in Salford, England
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought heat was a fluid called caloric, that could only flow from place to place. Joule showed that falling weights can make heat, at a fixed rate, so heat is a form of energy that movement can turn into.

quiz: A joule tells how much energy there is, and a watt tells how fast it moves.
Joules count the amount. One watt means one joule of energy moving every second.
A thing that holds more energy is always more powerful.
Power is how fast energy moves. A phone battery holds less than a chapati but gives its energy out much faster.
The energy a bulb uses is gone for ever once the light shines.
It moves into light and warmth in the room. Energy only changes form; it is never destroyed.
A 50 watt fan running 16 hours uses more energy than a 2000 watt geyser running 20 minutes.
Energy used is power times time. A weak appliance left on for long can use more than a strong one used briefly.
The number on a food label is exactly the energy your body gets.
How much you get depends on how food is cooked and chewed, and on tiny living beings in your gut.
Most of the energy in food ends up as warmth in the body and air.
Your body uses food energy to move and work, and nearly all of it finally spreads out as warmth.
Your body lets out the energy in a chapati all at once.
It lets energy out slowly, at about the pace of a bright bulb, so you can use it all day.
A machine turns only part of its energy into the form you want; the rest becomes warmth.
Some energy always spreads out as warmth, so no machine turns all of its energy into useful work.
A rating plate shows the least power an appliance will use.
A rating plate shows the most power the appliance will use, measured in watts.
Food, wood, coal and wind all get their energy from the Sun; nuclear and Earth's deep heat are exceptions.
Nearly all the energy we use can be traced back to sunlight, apart from nuclear energy and heat from deep in the Earth.
odd: Joules, kilojoules and kilocalories count how much energy there is; a watt says how fast it moves.
Watts say how fast energy is used; a kilowatt-hour counts how much energy was used over time.
A bulb's job is light, which is the useful energy; the warmth in glass, wire and air is spread-out energy.
Coal, wind and food all got their energy from sunlight; nuclear fuel did not.
